newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU softening on chips, wants technology deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU softening on chips, wants technology deal.

text.p: The European Union is softening its opposition to a U.S.-Japan semiconductor alliance in order to press for progress on a wider International Technology Agreement, EU sources said on Tuesday.
They said the European Commission -- which negotiates EU trade policy -- was backing down from an ultimatum that insists on EU inclusion in the chip alliance.

The move comes just two days before a meeting of trade officials from the United States, Canada, Japan and the EU in Seattle, Washington, where they are to discuss strategy ahead of December's World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore.
EU officials believe the Seattle meeting is the last chance for work to begin on an ITA before the WTO ministerial.

Sources said EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan wrote to his U.S. counterpart, Charlene Barshefsky, on Tuesday to reiterate his opposition to the alliance, but the delicately phrased letter gives her room to negotiate with U.S. producers for less damaging consequences for the European industry.
Washington and Tokyo signed an agreement in July which gives their respective semiconductor industries responsibilty for monitoring foreign access to their markets.
Brittan's letter is believed to accuse the U.S. and Japanese industries of "holding semiconductor trade hostage", but avoids direct criticism of governments.

The letter suggests that work on the ITA -- a hoped for agreement on technology trade between the EU, U.S. and Japan -- could begin if the "discriminatory aspects" of the chip alliance are not applied until after the ITA is finalised.
Sources say this implicitly calls for the semiconductor alliance to fall under some jurisdiction of an ITA, where the EU would have a voice.
Barshefsky last week accused to EU of backing down from its committment for an ITA, a charge Brittan has strongly refuted.

While seeking a way forward, the Commission is expected to launch its defense soon by suggesting U.S. trade negotiators may not have a mandate to agree product-specific cuts in tariffs and other barriers.
The Commission says it wants an ITA to cover wide range of technology products, but officials fear the U.S. is seeking to exclude certain items.

Industry analysts say Brittan has little choice but to call for a wide ITA, as this is the only way he can trade-off European tariffs on semiconductors against areas such as capacitors and photocopiers where European companies are more competitive.
The semiconductor alliance guarantees American chip producers at least 19 percent of the Japanese market, although in practise U.S. producers have enjoyed a greater share.
EU chip producers have just one percent of Japan's market, while U.S. and Japanese chip makers have a 66 percent share of the 15-nation bloc's sales.
